issues.legal_issue: A municipal tax on mobile towers falls within the State’s legislative authority to tax land and buildings when its substance and incidence are a tax on the land or building used for the tower.
material_facts: The towers comprised structures and telecommunications equipment installed on vacant land or on existing buildings under agreements with property owners.
The levy was calculated by reference to the yield from the land or building and was imposed on its use for a mobile tower, rather than on the use of the tower’s plant and machinery.
The cellular operators challenged the legislative competence to impose the tax, arguing that the towers were telecommunications apparatus.
issues.conclusion: The State legislature was competent to authorize the tax. A mobile tower used on land or a building can be treated as falling within the constitutional field of taxation on land and buildings, and the relevant levy was valid.
issues.legal_principle: Article 265 requires taxation to have authority of law, and Article 246 allocates legislative competence according to the Seventh Schedule. Entry 49 of List II is to be interpreted broadly and dynamically, not by reference to definitions in the challenged statute. A tax whose incidence is on land or a building may coexist with legislation concerning telecommunications where the tax is not on the telecommunications equipment itself. The Court relied on Anant Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Gujarat (1975) 2 SCC 175, Goodricke Group Ltd. v. State of W.B. (1995) 1 Supp SCC 707, Ajoy Kumar Mukherjee v. Local Board of Barpeta, AIR 1965 SC 1561, and Government of A.P. v. Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd., AIR 1975 SC 2037, as well as the principles of constitutional-entry interpretation discussed in Synthetics and Chemicals Ltd. v. State of U.P. (1990) 1 SCC 109, Good Year India Ltd. v. State of Haryana, AIR 1990 SC 781, State of West Bengal v. Kesoram Industries Ltd. (2004) 10 SCC 201, Trutuf Safety Glass Industries v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P. (2007) 7 SCC 242, India Cement v. State of Tamil Nadu (1990) 1 SCC 12, Jagannath Baksh Singh v. State of U.P., AIR 1962 SC 1563, and Elel Hotels & Investments Ltd. v. Union of India (1989) 3 SCC 698.

rule.if: municipal_tax_validity_challenge and mobile_tower_installed_on_land_or_building and levy_measured_by_property_yield and tax_incidence_is_property_not_equipment

predicates.municipal_tax_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a municipal tax imposed in connection with a mobile tower.
predicates.mobile_tower_installed_on_land_or_buildi: A mobile tower is installed on vacant land or on an existing building.
predicates.levy_measured_by_property_yield: The levy is measured by the yield or value attributable to the land or building used for the tower.
predicates.tax_incidence_is_property_not_equipment: The tax is imposed on the use of the land or building rather than on the use of the tower’s telecommunications equipment.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges a municipal tower-related tax, the tower is installed on land or a building, the levy is measured by the property’s yield, and its incidence is on the property rather than the equipment, the State may tax the tower as land or building.

issues.legal_issue: A writ challenge to a municipal tax should not be entertained where an applicable statutory alternative remedy is available, subject to issues left for determination by the appropriate forum.
material_facts: Cellular operators brought writ petitions challenging property-tax levies on mobile towers under the municipal legislation applicable in the Bombay cases.
The High Court declined to entertain those petitions because the operators had alternative remedies under the Act.
The Supreme Court left the operators free to raise the retrospective operation of the assessments or demands and their quantum before the appropriate forum.
issues.conclusion: The operators in the Bombay cases were to pursue the available statutory remedies rather than have their writ challenges entertained; questions concerning retrospective operation and the quantum of the tax were left open for the appropriate forum.
issues.legal_principle: Where a statute provides an alternative remedy, the aggrieved party may be required to pursue that remedy instead of seeking writ relief. The judgment left the retrospective operation of assessments or demands and the quantum of tax to the appropriate forum.

predicates.municipal_tax_writ_challenge: A party brings a writ proceeding challenging a municipal tax.
predicates.statutory_alternative_remedy_available: The governing statute provides the party with an alternative remedy for the tax dispute.

issues.definition: If a party brings a writ challenge to a municipal tax and a statutory alternative remedy is available, the writ challenge is not entertained and the party pursues that remedy.
